item.title: Cisco Enterprise Networking App for Splunk - v4.0.10 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
##### Compatibility and dashboards * **TA compatibility preflight:** Overview now confirms that Cisco Enterprise Networking Add-on for Splunk 4.0.0 or later is installed and that the complete transition-eventtype contract is available. Missing, older, or incomplete TA deployments receive a persistent warning. * **NetFlow search compatibility:** NetFlow searches, drilldowns, React search links, and data-model constraints use `eventtype=cisco_netflow`, covering production `stream:netflow` while excluding options metadata from Network Traffic scope. * **SD-WAN access migration compatibility:** ACL and SGACL searches and data-model constraints use `cisco_sdwan_acl_logs` and `cisco_sdwan_sgacl_logs`, preserving current and retained sourcetype history without broadening unrelated data-model children. * **Catalyst Center report migration compatibility:** Scheduled-report datasets use `cisco_dnac_inventory_report`, `cisco_dnac_compliance_report`, and `cisco_dnac_report` while retaining the existing dataset and field names. * **Dashboard correctness:** Invalid data-model fields, an undeclared Cyber Vision host token, empty drilldown conditions, incorrect Security Insights filters, and SD-WAN/Meraki Security Events time-series selectors were corrected. * **Bounded dashboard work:** The Security Events timeline now uses two data-model scans instead of three, top-N panels use bounded sorts, and discarded sort or aggregation stages were removed from trend searches. * **Navigation and branding:** Supported Splunk 10.4 navigation icons replace collapsed-menu letter monograms, and the packaged app icon and logo set align with the Cisco Enterprise Networking Add-on. * **Search contract audit:** Automated coverage now checks classic dashboards, Dashboard Studio definitions, and scheduled searches for macro, token, data-model field, index, acceleration, and bounded-search contracts. ##### Security and build tooling * **Patched dependency graph:** The Yarn dependency graph resolves the repository's current security advisories, removes the unused Lerna/Nx/npm publication subtree, and upgrades the packaging toolchain without adding `node_modules` to the installable Splunk app. * **Smaller build surface:** The lockfile was reduced from 1,296 to 849 package resolutions while retaining the TypeScript, Tailwind, React, and Splunk packaging workflow. Node.js 20.9 or later is required only for building the app, not for running the packaged Splunk app. ##### Upgrade notes * Install Cisco Enterprise Networking Add-on for Splunk **4.0.0** before App 4.0.0. The coordinated app depends on TA-owned transition eventtypes and does not bundle or redefine them. * Rebuild existing `Cisco_Catalyst_App` data-model acceleration summaries after upgrading both packages because the NetFlow, SD-WAN access, and Catalyst Center report constraints changed. * Keep `stream:netflow` in the app discovery macro and use `eventtype=cisco_netflow` in searches. * Generic Custom API data remains outside broad CIM children; select it by its stable product sourcetype plus `endpoint_name` or `endpoint_path`.


Short Description:
Dashboards and data models for Cisco enterprise networking data. Current installation, dependency, configuration, and troubleshooting instructions are in the User Guide included with Cisco Catalyst Add-on for Splunk (Splunkbase 7538).


Description:
Cisco Enterprise Networking for Splunk Platform provides dashboards and data models for Cisco Catalyst Center, Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN, Cisco Identity Services Engine (ISE), Cisco Cyber Vision, Cisco Meraki, Cisco ThousandEyes, supported Cisco network-device data, and NetFlow. Current installation, dependency, configuration, validation, and troubleshooting instructions are maintained in the User Guide included with Cisco Catalyst Add-on for Splunk (Splunkbase 7538). Release Notes:
**TrackMe 2.4.15 — Topology Studio maturity: views inside views, view integrity checks, a redesigned views browser, and Tenant Home stability at very high scale.** * **Views inside views — cross-view topologies.** A saved topology view can now be placed on another canvas as a **fourth node type**, next to entities, aggregates and labels. The referenced view keeps ownership of its graph and policies; the parent shows its live health (the worst effective state of the child’s health nodes, nested views included) and a KPI counting the unique underlying entities. View references are alertable, exportable and understood by **Build with AI** — the step from *a map* to *a map of maps*. See [Node types](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/product_guide/topology_overview.html#pg-topology-overview). * **TrackMe now watches the views themselves.** A new Configuration Guardian check detects views that reference deleted or disabled tenants, removed components or aggregates that no longer resolve — and the Topology Alerts silently broken by it. Affected views carry an integrity badge, an integrity panel explains every finding, and an editor banner offers **in-place remediation**. See [View integrity checks](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/product_guide/topology_integrity.html#pg-topology-integrity). * **A redesigned views browser.** **Cards**, **Compact cards** and a sortable **List** layout, a **category filter** combined with search, a deployment-wide default display mode set by administrators, and a per-user choice that persists. See [Views browser](https://docs.trackme-solutions.com/latest/product_guide/topology_views_browser.html#pg-topology-views-browser). * **A better editor.** Large views show a continuous loading progress instead of a greyed-out canvas; the inspector opens at a viewport-derived size and is clearly resizable; aggregate members gain **View status**, **View details** and **Open in Tenant Home** drilldowns; aggregates scale to **500 auto-generated members** with an independent auto-entities filter and a configurable **auto-arrange**. * **Topology Alerts honour global maintenance mode.** Enabling maintenance — immediate or scheduled, all tenants or a scope — freezes every Topology Alert whose selection touches a covered tenant: no phantom incidents or emails during the window. * **Tenant Home — stability at very high entity counts.** Deep browser-memory work removes repeated scans and retained datasets, parses large responses in batches, and preserves the last good data with a Retry when a refresh fails, so the browser tab stays healthy on very large tenants. * The release also brings image decoration background colours, a Guardian counter fix, two tenant metric-index fixes, and the cycle’s dependency refresh with four security updates. item.title: Adjutant AI (AI Workbench) - v2.5.3 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
# Adjutant AI (formerly AI Workbench) — Release notes What's new, improved, and fixed in each release, in plain language. This is the **customer-facing** summary used for the Splunkbase release-notes section; the full technical changelog lives in the project's detailed release notes. **Last updated:** 2026-09-07 > **About version numbers.** Releases once numbered 0.10–0.13 were renumbered to > 1.0–1.3 to reflect production maturity — no behaviour changed. The current release is > **2.5.3**, private LLM endpoints, on top of **2.5.2**'s one connection for several tenants and **2.5.1**'s fixes to **2.5.0**'s setup wizard and **2.4.2** — a data-correctness fix on top of **2.4.1**, a connectivity release on top of the **2.4.0** integration workstream and **2.2.2**, itself a maintenance release on **2.2.1**, itself a maintenance release on > **2.2.0**'s **Explain a SPL search**, and **2.1.0**'s **Fraud capability** and the **2.0 line** (the deterministic **ITSI Root > Cause Analysis** engine, **resource-consumption monitoring**, and **2.0.7**'s durable memory, > Scheduled Ask and governed integrations), which in turn built on > **1.8.5** (the **CIM Coverage Audit**), **1.8.4** (async playbook execution over MCP > plus the **Outcome Ledger** executive/audit dashboard), **1.8.3** > (a security‑hardening release: OWASP + dependency + anti‑ransomware audit), **1.8.2** (Splunk > Edge Processor data‑quality awareness and keyless Azure OpenAI authentication), **1.8.1** > (support‑diagnosis fixes) and **1.8.0** (agent telemetry & OCSF export, content packs, > all‑tiers data‑quality checks, Splunk 10.x readiness, Dashboard Studio version‑awareness). The > **1.7.0** ServiceNow integration and the **1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth"** themes are > included below. --- ## 2.5.3 "A private endpoint is a real endpoint" **If you connect an LLM over a private address, upgrade.** From a customer whose Azure OpenAI is published through an Azure Private Endpoint. ### An endpoint on your own private network is no longer refused Their service resolves, correctly and inside their network, to `10.228.105.42`. `curl` from the search head returned a completion. The wizard refused it. An Azure Private Endpoint, an AWS PrivateLink interface and an API gateway inside your VNet are all on private addresses by construction — that is what they are for. The setup checks refused every one of them, while the app's own runtime path called the same address without complaint. So the wizard was blocking a configuration the product supports, which is the worst way for a checker to be wrong. Loopback and link-local addresses are still refused, for every provider and every check. Those are the ones worth refusing: the cloud metadata service, and whatever is listening on 127.0.0.1 on your search head. A name that resolves to one public address and one loopback address is still refused too. ### It no longer sends you to your DNS team over a name that resolves The same screen said the name resolved to `10.228.105.42` and, a few lines later, that it had no record and the owner was your DNS team — with a ready-made ticket saying `Result: no record`. Every refusal the app made for its own reasons was being reported as a DNS failure. It now says what actually happened: **Refused by this app**, with the reason, and it says plainly that the name resolved, the network was never asked, and the fix is not with a network or DNS team. A genuine DNS failure still reports as one. --- ## 2.5.2 "One connection, several tenants" ### "OpenAI failed in a way this app does not recognise" That message was about us, printed where a sentence about your connection belonged, and there were two faults behind it. **The request was ours and it was malformed.** The credential check makes a real call on purpose, so it has to name a model. OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq, Gemini and OpenRouter never ask you for one, because a key alone completes them, and the check that reads the model list runs two steps later. So the call went out naming no model at all, and OpenAI rejected it. Each of those providers now has a cheap model it uses for that one check, and a model you chose is never overridden. Ollama is the exception and now asks for a model, because it serves only the models you have pulled and there is nothing safe to assume. Azure and Bedrock still ask, for the same reason: a deployment name is something only you know. **Then we could not name what came back.** The failure path consulted two of the three tables the app has and skipped the one that knows what an ordinary provider rejection is. It now uses all three, and it shows **what the provider said in its own words** alongside our reading of it, both on screen and in the support package, so the file can be used to check that the reading was right rather than only to repeat it. Credentials a provider echoes back inside its own error text are still removed before the file is written. And the message for a rejected request no longer guesses at the cause. It used to add that this "usually means the endpoint is for a different API than the one this app speaks" — on a run where the wizard had **confirmed the endpoint two checks earlier**, which sent the reader back to re-check the one thing already proved. It now says the credential was accepted and the request refused, and prints the provider's own reason underneath. ### Rechecking a connection no longer edits it behind your back Opening an existing connection in the wizard did not carry everything the record already held. The model, the api-version, the call mode and the list of Organisations and Business Units were all left behind, and each omission became a silent edit when you pressed Create. The tenant list is the one worth spelling out. An empty list means *everyone*, so rechecking a connection you had scoped to a single Business Unit would have opened it to the whole estate, without saying so. Nothing in the interface would have told you. The call mode caused the visible symptom: the record said `splunk_proxy`, the wizard's draft said nothing, and the last step reported that what was written did not match what was tested. It had matched. The two sides were filling in the blank differently. ### Rechecking a connection you already have no longer refuses to save it **Open in wizard** on any connection created before 2.5.0 ran all the checks, passed them, and then said the configuration could not be written. Nothing was wrong with it. The wizard was asking the KV Store to create a row that was already there, and the KV Store correctly refused. An existing connection is now updated. The update merges, so fields no wizard step knows about -- an Entra authority host, extra headers, a per-user assignment -- are kept rather than deleted to write a model name, and the creation date stays the date it was created. One related change you would only notice on a bad day: if an update fails, the credential you entered is no longer deleted. On a new connection that clean-up is right, because nothing is using the credential yet. On one that already exists, deleting it would take a working connection's key away to tidy up after a failed edit, so it is left, and the message says so instead of claiming a rollback that did not happen. ### The model comes from your account's own list, not from a name we shipped Where a provider does not ask you for a model, the wizard has to pick one for its checks. It used a name compiled into the app, and on the first real Anthropic account it met that name had been retired: the checks failed with "the model name is not one this account can use", about a model the customer had never chosen. A name shipped in an app has a shelf life; what your account lists today does not. The models check now picks from the list your credential can actually see, preferring the small, cheap end of the range, since the question being asked is two plus two. It never picks an embedding or speech model, which are listed and cannot answer a chat request. The rest of the checks then use that model, and it is what the connection is saved with. ### "Signing in: Failed" when the credential was fine The same run reported the sign-in check as failed. It had not failed. That check asks one thing, whether the provider accepts your credential, and a provider that does not accept one says so immediately without ever looking at a model name. To get as far as saying "no such model" it had already accepted the credential. A not-found model no longer fails that check when the model was the wizard's own choice; it records that the credential was accepted and lets the models check supply a real one. A model **you** typed and got wrong is still reported, because that is yours to fix. ### A connection that worked is no longer refused for a blank field The last check assembles the record and refused it when the model was empty, saying "nothing is wrong with the connection; the record is not complete". Both halves were true, and the field was one the wizard had filled in for itself moments earlier: the checks above it had answered a real question and made a real tool call using exactly that model. Where a provider never asks you for a model, the record now adopts the one the checks used, and step 4 shows it before you press Create. Azure and Bedrock still ask, because a deployment name is something only you know. ### The API key you typed is now the key that gets used **If you are on 2.5.0 or 2.5.1, upgrade.** In the wizard, the checks ran as far as "Asking what sign-in it wants" and then "Signing in" failed with *no credential was supplied*, while the key sat in the field above it. The field reported that something had been typed and did not keep the value, so every check past that point really was sent without a credential. The wizard was describing what it had sent accurately; nobody could tell that was what it meant. ### The support package now records what the checks found A package taken from a failed run listed the checks and nothing they observed: no outcome on any stage, and an empty evidence block for checks that had just reported the resolved addresses, a 404 and a 401 on screen. The browser was sending the row the screen was drawn from, whose field names differ from the ones the package is assembled from, so almost everything was dropped in silence. The package now carries each check's own result: what passed, what it found, how long it took, and the status each host answered with. A package that records only our conclusion cannot be used to check the conclusion, which is the main thing it is for. ### An LLM connection can now serve more than one Organisation Only an administrator can create or change an LLM connection, so the question a connection has to answer is not who may edit it but who may **use** it. That was a single Organisation and Business Unit, which meant an estate with four tenants sharing one OpenAI account needed four identical connections, four copies of the same key, and four things to rotate. A connection now lists **as many Org/BU pairs as you like**: * Naming an **Organisation on its own** covers every Business Unit in it. * Naming **several pairs** makes the connection usable by anyone in any one of them. * Naming **nothing** leaves it open to every Organisation and every Business Unit, which is the default and what most installs want. It is on both screens: the setup wizard's first step, and the plain connection form for administrators who do not use the wizard. Both write the same field and the same control is used in both places, because a second implementation of "what did the admin choose" is a second set of rules to get wrong. The old model also could not express one thing at all: **"only the DFLT Organisation"**. The short `DFLT` was doing double duty as a real tenant and as the wildcard meaning everybody, so one value meant both. It can be said now. **Nothing changes on upgrade.** A connection saved before 2.5.2 keeps exactly the reach it had: one scoped to an Org still serves that Org, and the shared bootstrap connection stays open to everyone. You only get the new behaviour on connections you edit. Membership is still resolved on the server from the caller's own Splunk roles, never from anything the browser sends, and the explicit per-user and per-role grants continue to work as overrides. --- ## 2.5.1 "The address nobody was asked for" A fix release for 2.5.0, from the first real run of the wizard against OpenAI. ### Choosing OpenAI and pasting a key failed on the first check **If you are on 2.5.0, upgrade.** Choose OpenAI, paste the API key, press test, and the first check failed with `scheme '' is not http or https`, above a paragraph explaining that loopback, private and link-local addresses are refused deliberately so the setup tool cannot be used to scan your network. Every sentence of that was true. None of it was about what had happened. OpenAI has one address, so the wizard asks for a key and nothing else, and its own step 1 ordering is built around that ("a key alone completes them"). Nothing then filled the address in. An empty address has no scheme, the guard that protects against server-side request forgery refuses anything that is not http or https, and the single code that refusal mapped to carries the scanning explanation. A correct mechanism, pointed at the wrong problem, on the screen whose entire purpose is to name the right one. Every provider with a fixed address now uses it: OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq, Gemini, OpenRouter and Ollama. An address pasted as a bare hostname is completed rather than refused. **The same defect was found in Bedrock, and it was worse there.** Bedrock's address is derived from the region rather than fixed, and only the three stages that spend money knew how to build it, so the two checks below them were testing an empty string. A Bedrock customer would have failed the very first check and never reached any of the fifteen refusals this app knows how to explain. The address is now derived in one place, and a test asserts the route the ladder proves is the host the later stages actually call. ### A missing address is no longer reported as a security refusal Three situations used to arrive as one message. They are now three, because the response to each is different: **no address supplied**, **that is not a URL**, and the original **this app will not send a server-side request there**, which keeps its wording because for a genuine loopback or private address it is exactly right. The first two say plainly that nothing has been sent anywhere. ### A run that stopped said it was still running When a check failed, the run stopped there, and every check below it stayed on "Waiting" for ever. The screen read that as still running, so the progress bar never finished, the Review step could not be reached, and the support package was withheld "until every check has finished" on a run that had already stopped. That is the one moment the support package is worth having. Checks below a failure now say **Not run**, the run is reported as finished, and the support package is available. "Not run" is deliberately distinct from "Skipped": a skipped check is one that did not apply to your setup, and a not-run check is one that never got its turn. --- ## 2.5.0 "Set it up, and know that it works" Connecting an LLM used to be a form, a saved row, and a hope. If it did not work you got one line back and no way to tell whose fault it was. This release replaces that with a setup wizard that checks the connection the whole way through, and says who can fix whatever it finds. ### The setup wizard **Settings, then Add LLM**, now opens a four step wizard: choose a service, enter the details, test the connection, review and create. The old form is still there behind "set it up manually instead", for administrators who already have all twenty three values and do not want to be walked through them. Ten checks run in order, each one budgeted so it finishes inside Splunk Web's own timeout, with a live checklist rather than a spinner. They prove, in order: the name resolves, the route is open, the browser can reach it where that matters, the endpoint is the provider it claims to be, the credential is accepted, the model list is readable, a real question comes back answered, and a real tool call is made and returned. That last pair is the point. A green tick that only means "the key is valid" is what most test buttons give you, and it is why a connection can pass a test and then fail on the first question. The wizard asks the model what two plus two is, checks the answer, then asks it to call a Splunk tool and checks that it did. ### It tells you who can fix it Every failure resolves to one of over a hundred and fifty recorded remedies. Each names what happened in your terms, **who can fix it**, roughly how long that usually takes, and where the checks resume once it is fixed. The wizard reruns from the earliest check the fix could have affected, not from the beginning. Where the fix belongs to somebody else, you get a block to paste into a ticket: source host with its address, destination with its address and port, the direction stated as outbound, the reason, and a reproducing `curl` with the credential replaced by a shell variable. A refused connection gets a **different** block with a different heading, because a refused connection means the route works and nothing is listening, and raising a firewall request for it wastes days. ### Corporate networks The wizard tries every host your connection needs against every route it could take: direct, the proxy you entered, and splunkd's own. It works out which hosts need the proxy and which must bypass it, writes both settings, and then proves them together, because a grid of green cells is not the same as a working configuration. It names the appliance in the way, where the appliance signs its own error pages. Squid, Blue Coat, Zscaler, Netskope, Cisco, Forcepoint, Palo Alto and others are recognised, so you learn that your own proxy refused you rather than that "something" did. ### Connection status on the list Every LLM configuration now carries a status: Working, Reachable, Working with a warning, Failed, Not checked, or Saved unverified. Each one carries its age and what it actually proved. Rendering never touches the network, so opening Settings is never slow because a provider is slow. A light check runs on a six hour schedule and costs nothing: no completion, no tokens, no invoice line. Credentials that expire are warned about at thirty, fourteen, seven, three and one days, and on the day. The mail channel is checked before it is relied on, because a warning nobody receives is worse than none. ### The support package On the test step there is a small button that builds a file you can inspect and send us. It carries the checks, the URLs with credentials masked, the versions, the provider, and what each appliance answered. It is built from a list of named fields rather than by redacting a blob, and it never contains a credential: request header values never travel, because a header value is a credential by construction. ### Known limits, stated plainly **Azure** is verified against real resources: four host forms including AI Foundry project endpoints, both API key and Entra service principal, and the audience proved rather than guessed. **AWS Bedrock** is complete and has been exercised against every refusal AWS returns, but no call has yet succeeded against a live account with model access. **Ollama** carries fewer recorded failure signatures than the other providers. ## 2.4.2 "One event per record" A fix for a data problem that looked, from the search bar, like nothing was wrong — and one that did not look like nothing at all. ### Every Ask failed with "Internal error" **If you are on 2.4.0 or 2.4.1, upgrade.** Asking anything returned `Internal error (ref …)`. The 2.4.0 reliability work rewrote the retry module in place rather than adding to it, which deleted the LLM call orchestrator — while its one caller, the proxy that **every** Ask goes through, still called it. The result was an `AttributeError` on every request, surfaced as a generic internal error with the real reason only in `splunkd.log`. The orchestrator is restored alongside the newer retry helper. The two are disjoint and stay that way: one is the writer's bounded per-request retry, the other is the provider fallback chain with its circuit breaker and per-attempt journal. `tests/test_llm_retry.py` covers the restored path and was failing on `import` for two releases, which is how this reached a release at all. ### Network-policy events were merged, not split When a device snapshot was stored to a Splunk index, every rule from that device arrived as a **single event** containing the whole batch of JSON records, instead of one event per rule. The same applied to the object, warning and snapshot families. Nothing announced it. The field list still showed `rule_id`, `action`, `source_values` and the rest, because Splunk extracts fields from the first JSON object in an event — so the fields you clicked on were real and correct. Only the **count** was wrong, and the counts the app itself reported were counts of records submitted, not of events landed. A `| stats count by device_id` over the rule source type therefore under-reported by however many rules a device had. The cause was a single character. `default/props.conf` declared the parsing rules under `[adjutant:network_policy:*]`, and props.conf applies its wildcard match language to `source::` and `host::` stanzas only — in a source-type stanza the `*` is literal, so the stanza matched nothing and the events fell back to Splunk's defaults. Each family now has its own stanza, and a `[source::itmip_llm_splunk_writer]` stanza backstops any source type added to that path in future. ### A policy field was colliding with one of Splunk's own Expanded policy tuples carry a field named `source` — and `source` is one of the fields Splunk defines on every event, where it names what wrote the record. Splunk does not overwrite on a collision, it **merges**, so `| table source` returned the policy's source address and `itmip_llm_splunk_writer` together in one cell, with nothing to say which was which. Fields whose names Splunk already owns are now written as `original_` — so that one is `original_source`. This applies to the **index** write only: the KV Store rows, the policy graph and the API keep the model's own names, because `source` is part of what a `tuple_id` is hashed from and renaming it there would move every tuple id ever issued. ### `source` and `host` said who wrote the event, not where the data came from Every network-policy event landed with `source = itmip_llm_splunk_writer` and `host = ai_workbench` — true of every event this app has ever written, and therefore no use for filtering or for a CIM-style view of where a policy came from. They now describe the input. `host` is the box the configuration was **read from**: the device or manager when it was reached over the network, and the Splunk instance itself when the input was a file or a paste, because that is the machine that held it. `source` names the input — a file path when the collector recorded one, else the file name, else `cisco:asa:config` for a device configuration or `cisco:fmc:api` for a manager collection. An FMC collection is labelled by the **manager**, not by the device platform it describes, which is the distinction the field is for. ### An Org with its own mapping collection saw an empty one — or someone else's An Org that registers a `mapping_collection` gets its own (`itmip_ai_mappings_`), which is the isolation boundary. The shipped example mappings were only ever seeded into `DFLT`'s, so that collection stayed **empty**: the examples were invisible to the Org, and an integration resolving its `mapping_ref` at run time under that Org found nothing. Compounding it, the Mappings tab did not tell the server which app it was in, so it resolved as the fallback Org and displayed **DFLT's** collection. An admin could Verify and Clear a mapping there, and a schedule running under their real Org would still refuse — pointing at a row in a collection nobody was looking at. The shipped examples are now seeded per Org, and the tab resolves the same Org the runtime does. **One consequence to know about:** mappings authored while the tab was mis-resolving live in the fallback Org's collection. They are not lost, but they belong to that Org and will not appear under yours. Re-create or re-scope anything you need. ### Seeded mappings could never be corrected after the first install A seeded mapping is documented as re-seed-eligible: ship a fix, and an untouched system-owned row picks it up. It never worked. The seeder POSTed to the KV Store collection root, which only ever **inserts** — splunkd answers `409` for a `_key` that already exists and leaves the row alone — and the 409 landed in a bare `except: pass`. Every correction to a shipped mapping since the first install was silently dropped. A second guard compounded it: the seeder skipped any row cleared for unattended use. That was added for a real reason (restarts were resetting clearance) but it froze the whole row rather than the decision, so the mapping most likely to run unattended was the one fixes could never reach. On a real instance the shipped Cisco ASA mapping was still at its pre-B3.3 shape: **no `device_id` in the projection** and **no `source.schema_version`**, so the writer's schema pin had nothing to compare and could not refuse a batch the mapping would silently strip of its NAT view. The refusal that exists to prevent exactly that could not fire. Now: the seeder replaces then inserts, so corrections land; and clearance is carried across an unchanged re-seed but **revoked when the content actually changed**, recording who had cleared it and why it was revoked. A human cleared a specific mapping, not a name — so a changed mapping stops and asks, instead of running under an approval that no longer describes it. ### The shipped ASA Playbook pointed at a superseded mapping "Cisco ASA Policy Ingestion (mapping-driven)" was wired to `cisco-asa-config-to-network-policy-v1`, which is `superseded_by` v2 and pinned to source schema 1.0. The pipeline has emitted 2.0 since the NAT work, so a run through it is refused with `schema_version_mismatch` — and the refusal names v2, meaning the product was telling operators to fix a wiring mistake the product shipped with. The Playbook now names v2. The trailing `-v1` / `-v2` in a mapping name is its **schema generation**, not its lifecycle version; a mapping carries its own `operational v1` separately. Two axes, one letter. The Playbook's mapping picker now shows each mapping's title alongside its ref (the Mappings tab lists them by title, so the same mapping looked like two different objects), flags a superseded choice with the successor's name before you save, and spells out that clearing for unattended is a separate step from promoting. ### Policy records were stamped with the wrong Org and BU Run a network-policy ingestion from the Ask tab in a host app such as `itmip_fis_app`, with the header showing your real Org and BU, and every landed record still said `tenant_org: DFLT`, `tenant_bu: DFLT`. Org and BU are resolved server-side from the caller's roles **and** the app they are working in. The Ask request itself sends that app; the tool dispatch behind it did not, so resolution fell back to the assistant app's own name — which matches whichever Org registered *that* pattern, not the one the user is in. An Org whose `app_patterns` name the host app could never match. The netpol, `splunk_memory` and `splunk_mapping` tool calls now send the host app. This is a context hint, not a grant — an Org matches only when the caller's real roles also match its `role_patterns` — so it cannot widen anyone's access; it makes tenant data land under the tenant it belongs to. Records written on 2.4.0 or 2.4.1 through these tools carry the fallback Org/BU and are not corrected retroactively. **This one is in the frontend bundle**, so hard-refresh the browser after upgrading. ### Security: raw firewall configurations were readable by every authenticated user `itmip_netpol_artifacts` stores collected configurations as base64. Redaction on the import path is opt-in, so unless it was asked for, a stored artifact still contains the secrets the scanner merely counted — on our own sample config, an enable-password hash and two IKEv2 pre-shared keys. That collection had no ACL of its own, so it inherited the app default of `read : [ * ]`. Every protection the artifact store provides — tenant scoping, an owner check, metadata-only reads, a download link that expires in an hour — guards the REST path; a direct KV Store read from a lookup command or the Lookup Editor went around all of it. `itmip_netpol_artifacts`, `itmip_netpol_parses` and `itmip_netpol_snapshots` are now **admin / sc_admin** read and write. No functional change: every netpol read goes through the endpoint's system token, and that endpoint was already admin-gated. The published policy collections (`itmip_network_policy_rules_current` and its siblings) stay readable — they hold modelled policy rather than credentials, and searching them is the product. **If you have run a collection on 2.4.0 or 2.4.1**, treat any credential in a collected config as having been readable by any app user for the artifact's 7-day retention, and rotate accordingly. ### Warnings you can trace back to what they are about A network-policy warning carried `code`, `message` and `line` — a sentence, and no way to go and look. `line` also answers nothing for an API collection, which has objects rather than lines. Warning events now carry `refs{}` (the ACL name, the object id, the uuid an FMC rule referenced — identifiers the parser had already collected and the index write was discarding), `evidence_ref` in the same `#L` form that rules use for `raw_evidence_refs`, and `artifact_id`. One idiom now locates a warning and a rule alike. The offending configuration line itself is still never carried into an index — it stays in the protected, secret-scanned artifact, and the evidence ref is how you reach it. ### Duplicate warnings on the same collection Warnings from an FMC collection are built per rule side, so two access rules referencing the same uncollected port object produced the same warning twice — and the indexed warning event carries `code`, `message` and `line` and nothing else, so the copies were indistinguishable and the repetition told you nothing. Byte-identical warnings now collapse to one; anything that differs, even by a line number, is still two warnings. Warnings are not part of a snapshot's semantic hash, so no snapshot is re-identified by this. ### OCSF telemetry took its timestamp from ingest time `[ocsf:itmip:*]` had the same defect, so agent-telemetry events were timestamped when Splunk received them rather than from the `time` field in the OCSF envelope. On a busy or delayed pipeline that moves events on the timeline. One stanza per OCSF class now. **Upgrading.** These are index-time settings: they apply to events indexed **after** a splunkd restart, and events already in the index stay merged. To correct history, remove the affected events and re-store the snapshots. --- ## 2.4.1 "Getting connected" Everything here came out of two customer setups in the same fortnight: an Azure OpenAI service published through a corporate API gateway, and one behind a private endpoint. Both stalled in the same place. The credentials were right, the firewall was open, the built-in connection test was green — and every question still failed. The release is about closing the distance between "the test passes" and "it works", and about not making an administrator assemble a URL by hand from three values nobody gave them. ### Find my endpoint (Azure OpenAI) Azure needs the complete address of a deployment, not the address of the service: everything up to and including `/chat/completions`, with the deployment name and an api-version in it. Behind a gateway that address also carries a path prefix chosen by whoever publishes the API. An administrator is typically handed a base URL and expected to work out the other three parts, and getting any of them wrong produces a "Resource not found" that reads like a permissions problem. There is now a **Find my endpoint** button beneath the endpoint field. Give it whatever you were given — often just the hostname — and it works out the rest from the Splunk server itself, then offers to fill in the endpoint, the deployment and the api-version in one click. Where the service lists its deployments, it also shows you every deployment it found together with the model behind each one, which answers a question customers ask constantly: the deployment is named `gpt-4o`, but is that actually what runs? It finds the address by paying attention to *how* each attempt is refused rather than just that it failed. A gateway refusing an address it does not publish answers differently from Azure refusing a deployment name it does not have, and the second kind of refusal proves the rest of the address is already right. When it cannot finish the job it says exactly what is still missing instead of failing vaguely — most usefully "the address and version are confirmed, the deployment name is not", which turns a five-part question for the API team into a one-part question. It also recognises a service that speaks the OpenAI dialect rather than the Azure one, and tells you to change provider instead of leaving you to guess. It runs only when you press it, and it is capped so it cannot flood anyone's gateway. ### Test connection now reports on the address, not just the login The connection test could report success on a configuration that no question would ever work against. It checked whether the credential was accepted, and an address that answers "not found" still accepts a credential — so a wrong address passed the test and failed every time it was used. That combination sent at least one administrator hunting through firewall rules for an afternoon. It now reports the two things separately. When the address does not work it says so plainly, and distinguishes the two reasons — an address that was left as the service base, or a deployment name that does not exist. When everything is right, it names the model that answered. ### Proxy exceptions, per configuration Reaching Microsoft to sign in and reaching the AI service are two different destinations, and in a locked-down network they often need opposite treatment: the corporate proxy is the only way out to Microsoft, while the service itself answers only on a direct connection. Until now a configuration had one proxy setting for both, so whichever you chose broke the other, and the only workaround changed proxy behaviour for every Splunk process on the machine. Configurations that use a proxy can now list the hosts that must bypass it. Sign-in goes through the proxy, the AI service is reached directly, nothing else on the server is affected, and the change takes effect when you save rather than when you restart. ### Fixed - **Model discovery found nothing behind an API gateway.** The lookup rebuilt the address from the hostname alone and threw away the path prefix, so it asked the wrong place and quietly reported no models. It now keeps the prefix. - **Deployments with your own naming lost their cost figures.** A deployment named for your estate rather than for the model — `acme-gpt4o-prod` — is not a name the price list knows, so usage was recorded with no money against it. The model that actually answered is now recorded alongside the configured name and used for pricing when the configured name is unknown, so those deployments cost correctly. Where the two differ, both are kept. - **A licence that could never be activated said "re-activate".** A key issued with no device limit records no activations at all, so a node-locked tier can never be satisfied by it and pressing re-activate cannot help. The licence page now says the key was issued without a device limit and needs reissuing, instead of sending administrators round a loop that had no exit. --- ## 2.2.2 "Finish the dashboard" A maintenance release about one thing: runs that did all the work and then ended with nothing on the glass. Every item came from watching real dashboard builds on a live estate, and in each case the assistant's own safety check was the reason the dashboard never appeared. The check was right about the problem and wrong about what to do next — it refused, gave instructions, and the instructions either could not be carried out or cost more of the run's budget than was left. ### Fixed - **Dashboards that were refused are now repaired instead.** When two panels ran the same underlying search, the assistant used to stop and describe a three-step manual fix. The fix is mechanical, so the builder now performs it: it creates the shared search once, points both panels at it, and keeps the fields those panels need. Your dashboards get the efficient shape without the run being interrupted, and the same search no longer runs twice. - **Panels that came back empty next to a search that clearly had data.** When a shared search was widened more than once to serve different panels, each widening discarded the previous one. On one nine-panel dashboard five panels showed "No results found" while the search behind them returned the right events. The widenings now combine. - **A check that asked for the impossible.** A panel that calculates its own value — a formatted date, a derived score — was refused for not finding that value in the shared search, where it cannot exist, because the panel computes it afterwards. Values a panel makes for itself are no longer demanded of the search. The related guidance was also wrong in a way that mattered: panels sharing a search are siblings, not a sequence, so a value one panel calculates is invisible to the others and has to be calculated where all of them can see it. - **A failed publish threw away the work it told you to fix.** The message on a validation failure said the dashboard was still open for editing and warned against starting over. It had in fact been discarded, so the repair failed and the assistant rebuilt every panel from scratch — which on one run quietly changed a correct detection into a different one. The dashboard now genuinely stays open when publishing fails. - **One special character could cost an entire dashboard.** A "≥" written as `≥` in a panel's explanatory text made the whole dashboard invalid, discarding a run of around forty steps that had already produced four working searches. Special characters in text are now handled safely no matter which one is used. - **An empty shared-search reference was treated as a real one**, producing a confusing refusal at publish time that asked for a search with a blank name. ### Improved - **Detections are now held to what you asked for.** New guidance covers the ways a detection can look perfect and point at the wrong event — quietly matching a wider set of events than you described, being loosened until it finally returns a row, discarding the field that distinguishes one event type from another, or dropping the amounts and account numbers an analyst needs before the result reaches the table. A rule that renders beautifully and flags the wrong event is worse than one that returns nothing, because nothing looks broken and nobody checks. The assistant now reads its own result back against the raw events before handing it to you. - **"No results" is no longer accepted as proof a detection works.** For a rule whose job is to match something, an empty result proves only that the syntax is valid — "this does not happen in your data" and "this rule cannot detect it" look identical. The assistant now establishes which of the two it is found before telling you, and runs over a period that actually covers the evidence it has already located. - **Sequence detections ("A, then B, then C") are built correctly.** A common shortcut for expressing order silently sorts alphabetically instead of by time, which can make a rule return nothing on a textbook-perfect match. Existing private playbooks you authored are unaffected; the old entries are retired so you are not offered both. --- ## 2.2.1 "Proven" A maintenance release, and every item in it came from running 2.2.0 against a real estate rather than from reading the code. One new capability came along with the fixes. ### Fraud rings your risk threshold cannot see (Enterprise, fraud-analytics) Risk-based alerting adds up one entity's score across many events. A fraud ring is the opposite shape: many entities sharing one thing. Because those are different questions, no amount of threshold tuning finds a ring. Seventeen mule accounts each earning fifteen points against a threshold of forty are seventeen well-behaved customers, since the risk was split seventeen ways and no single account ever crossed. Lower the threshold and you get seventeen false positives, not one ring. This release adds the query that asks the other question: group by the shared attribute instead of by the account. Nothing new has to be collected, because fraud risk rules have always recorded the linking attribute alongside the score. It simply was never read back this way. It is rarity-weighted, which matters more than it sounds. Ask only "what is shared" and the answer is always the corporate proxy that everybody sits behind. Shared attributes are ranked the same way the Fraud Ring Mapper ranks them, so a shared password hash and a shared IP are never treated as equal evidence, and values that are simply infrastructure are shown separately rather than quietly removed — a short list should not be mistaken for a clean estate. It is also honest about one thing it cannot know. It counts accounts that some rule already scored, which is not the same as how many accounts exist that share the value. So it hands you the search that settles it against your real data, and until you run that, it labels its own confidence as provisional instead of guessing. If you cannot name a starting account, the Fraud Ring Mapper will now find candidates for you before it starts walking. ### Fixed - **Money laundering was graded ready on two weeks of data.** Structuring is a run of individually unremarkable deposits and layering is a graph, so neither is visible in a short window however complete the feed is. Our own use case catalogue has always said to grade retention as well as fields; the grader printed that note and never acted on it. History is now graded, and a use case whose data does not go back far enough is capped at partial with the shortfall named. It is worth separating from other gaps, because it is the one you close with a retention policy rather than an onboarding project. On our demo estate this moved money laundering from ready to partial. - **Every ServiceNow tool call failed** with an internal error reference and no explanation. A tenant lookup returned a dictionary and the calling code expected a pair. - **The fraud readiness dashboard.** Four defects, found by running it rather than reading it. The readiness lookup was private to our own app, so when a dashboard was generated into a customer app the summary panel could not resolve it and rendered empty — which reads as "nothing has been graded" rather than "you cannot see it from here". The audit's own verdicts were being re-graded on the way to the screen, so nine computed verdicts became eight different ones. The coverage audit could not reach the dashboard builder at all, so nothing enforced that a panel must return data before it goes on the glass, and an empty panel on a fraud dashboard is read as "nothing wrong". And no fraud dashboard mentioned data quality: no ingestion check, no TrackMe, no Cribl or Edge Processor. A readiness grade computed over a feed that is arriving late or half delivered is a confident answer about the wrong data, and it fails towards "you are ready". That panel is now mandatory and appears even when everything is clean, because "we checked and it is healthy" is a finding. - **Asking for a readiness audit in plain English now reaches the readiness audit.** The question our own demo guide tells people to ask did not route to the playbook it names. - **Fraud verdict columns are coloured.** Ready, partial and blocked — and the feed inventory's present and absent — were missing from the status colour map, so those columns could only be coloured by hand and often were not. - **A dashboard opened from a finished session sat on "Loading..."** until you refreshed the tab. Validation now runs first, so the prompt only appears for writes that can actually happen. - **Token and cost accounting missed cached tokens.** With prompt caching the provider reports only the uncached part of the input, so an agentic run showed a few thousand tokens next to a cost that looked impossible. Cached tokens are now recorded, priced and shown. This affected what we reported, never what you were charged. - **Test Connection for Azure could only ever time out on a broken network.** Its own retries outlasted the window Splunk Web allows, so you got a bare 504 instead of the staged diagnostic. Results are now bounded before they enter the conversation. --- ## 2.2.0 "Explain" ### Explain a SPL search — free on every tier Point it at a search and get back an explanation you keep. It compares an entity against its own history, or against its peer group, which the retiring app could not do. What we took from the retiring apps is their METHOD, not a dependency on them: the risk-contribution model, the behavioural profiling pattern, the entity pivots and the fraud use case catalogue are all reimplemented here and improved. If you do still run either app, importers can lift what you built into the native form, but that is a convenience rather than the point. - **The fraud patterns it now knows.** Signup fraud (many accounts sharing an email, IP, phone, password or bank account), account takeover (brute force against credential stuffing, one address against many accounts, impossible travel, and the profile-change-then-money-movement chain), money laundering (funds converging then dispersing, amounts kept just under a reporting threshold, sanctioned-country exposure), and two narrow verticals in unemployment-insurance claims and controlled-substance diversion. Both start by checking the data is actually flowing before offering any verdict, because a quiet fraud queue is either good news or a dead feed, and you should know which.
