The demonstration dataset has no licence requirement at all, so a trial environment always works. One thing said plainly: Adjutant AI is not a fraud detection engine and does not try to be. It will not decline a card payment in a hundred milliseconds; that is what the dedicated engines are for. It is the layer above them that finds what they miss across channels, connects the entities they cannot, and turns three weeks of investigation into an afternoon with a trail you can hand to an auditor. ## 2.0.7 "Memory, Scheduled Ask & Integrations" Adjutant AI gains a durable memory, a scheduled/unattended surface, and a governed data-integration subsystem — so it stops re-asking, can run on a clock, and can sync a system of record into Splunk under a contract two humans have reviewed. - **Memory — it stops re-asking.** A small, durable, per-tenant memory: **learned facts** (the index a report uses, what "the Cribl search" means for a team) captured the moment they're learned, and **integration watermarks**. Two new Knowledge tabs — **Learned Knowledge** (a confirm queue; promote a fact to the whole Org) and **Integration State** (force a watermark to replay or skip). Unattended runs use **confirmed facts only**; a captured-but-unconfirmed fact can't silently steer a run that writes to a target. Backed up per Org with the daily KV Store backup; a content-pack upload never overwrites it. - **"Templates" are now "Playbooks."** A presentation rename that finishes an inconsistency the engine already had (the alert action was always "Run Investigation Playbook"). No data migration. Explicit **run-mode tags** (`triggered` / `scheduled` / `integration`) replace the old bare `playbook` tag. - **Scheduled Ask.** A new admin tab to run a Playbook on a cron schedule — a **Scheduled Job** (run and deliver a result; Professional+) or a **Scheduled Integration** (read a source, write a target, keep watermarks; `ai-integration` feature). Each is a private, service-account-owned saved search that just *triggers* a governed, single-flighted, bounded run — no per-member scheduler racing over shared state (the DB-Connect-on-search-head-cluster lesson applied). - **Governed integrations.** A **mapping spec** is the contract: a versioned, declarative, lint-checked `source → transforms → destination` record the runner executes deterministically — the model never transforms rows. Author it in the new **Mappings** tab (a visual three-pane pipeline editor with a live sample rail, or JSON), promote it **4-eyes**, and **earn** unattended clearance after a verified run. Schema **drift** is detected deterministically, diagnosed by the assistant, and decided by a human — never a silent rewrite. Records land via **`splunk_writer`** (KV Store / CSV / HEC / spool, per-record routing, a fail-closed destination allowlist from the contract). Two ServiceNow example mappings and a standard mapping-driven integration Playbook ship to clone and parameterize. See `docs/ADJUTANT_MEMORY_AND_SCHEDULED_ASK.md` for the operator guide. ## 2.0.6 "ITSI RCA — Industrialise" The Root Cause Analysis engine reaches its industrialise milestone, and the smaller items deferred from earlier trains are completed. All analysis-only and off by default. - **Recovery verification** — after RCA names a cause, re-check whether the service actually recovered (which corroborates the cause) or is still degraded / newly regressed elsewhere. - **Calibrated confidence** — where enough analyst feedback exists, the engine shows a genuinely calibrated likelihood for a candidate instead of a raw internal score; until then it keeps the existing strength wording (never a made-up number). - **Draft, recommend-only remediations** — RCA can produce reviewable draft fixes routed by cause (restore the feed on the culprit host, fix onboarding/timestamp config, restart a stalled input, correct the monitoring, look upstream, add a KPI). Always a suggestion — never executed. - **Data-driven playbook** — the RCA phase sequence is now a validated, dependency-checked contract rather than a hardcoded list (same order, now extensible). - **Sharper feed diagnosis** — names which forwarder/HEC/pipeline host is the culprit, and adds dedicated Cribl and Edge Processor pipeline-health checks. - **Better lineage & safety** — resolves raw host/IP to canonical ITSI entities via declared aliases; follows saved-search/eventtype references inside subsearches; and hardens the unattended template so it can only follow the unattended procedure. --- ## 2.0.5 "Resource-consumption monitoring" A clear, per-tenant answer to *"how much does Adjutant AI cost to run?"* - **New "Resource Consumption" dashboard** shows the CPU, memory, threads and Splunk search-slots Adjutant AI uses — broken down **by Org and by Org/Business-Unit** and by workload (interactive Ask, unattended RCA, unattended runs, and — soon — scheduled Asks). - **Real per-run measurements.** Unattended work runs in its own process, so the app now records actual CPU-seconds, peak memory and thread counts for each RCA cycle and each automation run, tagged with the Org/BU it ran for. The numbers are content-free (counters only) and always on. - **Honest by design.** Interactive Ask runs inside Splunk's shared handler, where memory can't be pinned to one tenant — so for Ask the dashboard reports search CPU/slots (from Splunk's own audit log, mapped to Org/BU) and token/cost usage, and says so plainly, instead of inventing a figure. Additive and safe; no change to how analyses behave. --- ## 2.0.4 "ITSI RCA — discovery & external fold-in" The ITSI Root Cause Analysis engine completes its discovery train: - **Latent-dependency discovery** surfaces a likely service dependency that isn't declared in your ITSI topology but shows up in the data (shared inputs/entities, at-the-same-moment degradation) — proposed as a ready-to-review suggestion, never created automatically. - **External-AI fold-in** can consult an external AI provider's read of the incident and weigh it in as corroborating evidence — it can strengthen or temper a finding, but never overrides the engine's own deterministic verdict. Analysis-only and off by default. --- ## 2.0.3 "ITSI RCA — data-supply legs" The ITSI Root Cause Analysis engine learns to read a KPI's **data supply chain as distinct legs**: - It classifies where a KPI's data actually comes from — a DB Connect input, a universal forwarder, HEC, an Edge Processor / Cribl pipeline, syslog, or a scripted input — and shows which leg carries the most data ("the largest bar"). - When a feed problem occurs, it can point at the **specific leg** that failed (for example "the DB Connect leg stalled") instead of just flagging the whole index. - Behaviour-drift baselines can now be **seasonal** (same time last week) as well as the 7-days-prior default, so normal weekly patterns aren't mistaken for problems. Analysis-only; changes nothing about how the engine behaves until you opt in. --- ## 2.0.2 "ITSI RCA — KPI Behaviour Analysis" The ITSI Root Cause Analysis engine learns to read **how your KPIs are behaving**, not just whether they are red: - **Every KPI, including healthy ones, is profiled for behaviour drift** — a meaningful shift in a KPI's value that its own red/green threshold may miss (for example, response time slowly creeping up after debug logging was accidentally left on). - **Entity-level behaviour** pinpoints *which* entities are driving a service's degradation, not just that the service is unhealthy. - **Suggested-KPI recommendations**: where the analysis finds a blind spot the current KPIs don't measure, it proposes a monitoring improvement — always a suggestion, never a root-cause claim. All of this is analysis-only and off by default; it changes nothing about how the engine behaves until you opt in. --- ## 2.0.1 "Unattended engine hardening" The unattended investigation engine (the part of Adjutant AI that can investigate an alert with no human watching) is designed to hand the alert back to Splunk immediately and do the work in the background. That is what keeps your alerts fast — but it also means nobody is watching if a background run misbehaves. This release makes sure a misbehaving run always stops, and that you can see it when one does. The engine still ships **switched off**. If you have never enabled it, nothing changes for you. **Fixed** - **A run that keeps failing now gives up instead of restarting forever.** If a background run died, it was put back in the queue and started again — without counting how many times it had already failed. A run that failed every time (a bad playbook, a bug) could restart indefinitely and keep occupying a worker. Runs are now retried a set number of times and then parked as "given up", where they stop consuming anything and wait for a person. - **The per-run time limit now actually applies.** The "maximum time for one run" setting was shown in the configuration, charted on the dashboard and alerted on — but nothing enforced it. Runs now stop when they reach it. - **A stuck run is stopped, not just forgotten.** Previously the engine handed the work to a new run but left the stuck one alive, so two runs could work on the same alert and both spend money. The stuck one is now stopped first. - **Long, healthy runs are no longer interrupted.** A slow-but-fine run could be mistaken for a dead one and restarted underneath itself. Runs now report that they are alive continuously rather than only between steps. **New** - **Limits that protect Splunk itself.** A background run now caps its own memory, CPU and priority, so a runaway run degrades into one failed investigation instead of putting the Splunk platform under pressure. Sensible defaults are set for you; all are adjustable, and each can be switched off. - **You can now see stuck and given-up runs.** A run only reports on itself when it finishes, so runs that got stuck were invisible on every dashboard. The *Pipeline Knobs* dashboard has a new run-health section (stuck runs, given-up runs, runs being retried, and what each worker is doing), and two new optional alerts — **Runner stuck** and **Runs dead-lettered** — tell you without anyone having to look. Both are off by default. **Changed** - The retry setting is now called **`runner_max_attempts`** (it covers every kind of failure, not only runaway runs). The unused `retain_completed_hours` setting has been removed — run history retention is controlled by `queue_retention`. If you set either in a local override, update it. --- ## 1.8.5 "CIM Coverage Audit" When a data source is onboarded but a correlation search in Enterprise Security still comes back empty, or an ITSI KPI never fills, the cause is almost always that the source is not properly mapped to the CIM data model the search depends on. Finding out why is normally a slow, manual walk through the layers. The CIM Coverage Audit does it for you, from your real events and your real search head configuration. **New** - **Audit a sourcetype against a CIM dataset.** Ask, for example, audit cisco:asa against the Network Traffic All_Traffic dataset. You get back how much of the dataset the source covers, and if it does not, which layer is broken: the source is not tagged so the model cannot see it, its index is not on the model's allowlist, a field is missing or under the wrong name, a value needs normalizing, or the accelerated summaries the correlation searches read have not caught up. That last one is the confusing case where CIM works when you test it by hand but your correlation searches fire nothing, and the audit calls it out plainly. - **A fix you can read and deploy.** For each gap the audit produces the exact configuration, checked for validity, shown as your current stanza next to the proposed one, with a note on where it belongs. It never deploys anything itself. You review and apply it, which is what lets you run this where an automatic write to production would never pass change control. - **Honest about what a search head can see.** Adjutant AI runs on the search head, so it reads your search time configuration and the real events, and it is upfront that it cannot read the index time configuration on your indexers. It runs its searches as you, so it can never read data from an index you could not otherwise search. - Three read only helpers to read a sourcetype's search head props and transforms and check where a sourcetype has data. The diagnosis is available on Professional so any platform team can see which layer is broken. Generating the validated fix is an Enterprise feature. It grades against the CIM add on actually installed on your search head. Restart Splunk after upgrading. **Fixed** - **The app opens on the Ask tab again.** If your LLM runs entirely on the search head, with the key held server side (the Splunk proxy mode, an Azure managed identity, or a Bedrock role), the browser never receives an API key. The app used to read that as nothing being configured and jumped to the Settings tab on every launch. It now opens on Ask as intended, and only sends you to Settings when a key really is needed and missing. - **Clearer license status.** When a license is installed but the app cannot confirm it is active on this environment, it now tells you that directly instead of quietly dropping to the free Personal tier. Admins get a pointer to the License page to re-activate. --- ## 1.8.4 "Async playbooks over MCP" Run Adjutant AI playbooks from an AI agent over the Model Context Protocol with a reliable **start → poll → fetch** pattern. A playbook can take several minutes, but AI tool calls are subject to short timeouts you don't control (the MCP server, the client, proxies), so trying to wait for the answer in one call is fragile. Now every call returns in seconds. **New / Improved** - **Start returns immediately.** `adjutantai_start_playbook` (the old `adjutantai_run_playbook` name is removed) hands back a run id at once with a hint on how to poll. - **Check progress** with `adjutantai_get_playbook_status` — queued, running, completed, or failed (a run that hit a recoverable error and is auto‑retrying is reported as still running, not failed), with guidance to stop polling after ~15 minutes. - **Fetch the verdict** with `adjutantai_get_playbook_results` once completed — condensed by default, or the full result on request; a partial result is clearly labelled. - **Tenant‑safe.** One team can't read another team's run; unknown or expired run ids simply return "not found." Run records are kept for 7 days by default. - **Try it out of the box:** start `MCP Example: Read-only Health Check` under Org/BU `DFLT/DFLT` (the read‑only reference playbook shipped on every install), then poll and fetch. Requires the inbound MCP server and the Backend Ask Service to be enabled. No configuration changes. Restart Splunk after upgrading. ### Also in 1.8.4 — the Outcome Ledger (Enterprise) A single screen that answers what a CEO, CISO or auditor actually asks: *what did agentic AI do for us this period, was it any good, what did it save, what did it cost — and can I see the evidence for one run?* It assembles data the app already records (unattended‑run history, analyst agreement, run telemetry, LLM spend) into one executive/audit view. It adds **no new data collection and sends nothing to any external service.** **New** - **The dashboard** (`Adjutant AI ▸ Outcome Ledger`): headline tiles (investigations run without a human, how often analysts agreed with the AI — with the sample size and coverage shown, benign/false‑positive runs auto‑closed, analyst hours saved, LLM spend, typical time to a verdict), the mix of AI conclusions over time, agreement by case type, a weekly ledger, and an **evidence** table you can click through to the full detail of any single run. A footer spells out every assumption so a number is never quoted out of context. - **Safe to hand to an auditor.** What each viewer may see is decided on the server from their own identity — never from the page — and fails closed. In this release the dashboard is for Splunk administrators; scoped, delegated auditor access is the next step. - **Is the AI real, or just performing?** An Efficacy Trend panel puts run volume against how often analysts agreed, over time. If the agent runs more while analysts increasingly override it, the panel says so ("scaling faster than trust") instead of hiding it behind a healthy‑looking headline — and on too little feedback it honestly says the sample is too thin to judge. - **Honest numbers.** Effort saved is shown as time (with the per‑case assumption stated), spend is the real logged cost, and the per‑investigation efficiency signal is token usage — never an invented cost estimate. Enterprise feature. No effect on any existing behaviour. Restart Splunk after upgrading. --- ## 1.8.3 "Security hardening" A security‑focused release. Adjutant AI was put through an independent OWASP Top 10 (web **and** LLM), dependency‑vulnerability, and "AI‑driven ransomware" review. The headline: **no critical issues, no default passwords or keys, no vulnerable components that ship to you, and the assistant cannot be turned into an attack tool.** Confirmed issues are fixed; a plain‑language, reviewer‑ready write‑up ships in the app as `SECURITY_AUDIT.md`. **Improved / Fixed** - **Credentials stay server‑side.** Provider API keys and keyless Azure sign‑in secrets are never sent to the browser or to other users in your tenant. (The free‑tier browser API‑key path is unchanged.) - **Prompts stay in your audit index**, not Splunk's internal logs. - **Stronger multi‑tenant isolation** for investigation results and knowledge sources. - **You confirm every change.** Closing a notable, setting a disposition, an ITSI/TrackMe/ServiceNow write, or overwriting a saved dashboard now asks for explicit confirmation first. Read‑only questions and new private dashboards are unaffected. - **General hardening:** cleaner errors, tighter sign‑in redirects, safer content‑pack imports, email TLS verification on by default. No new features or config changes. Restart Splunk after upgrading. --- ## 1.8.2 "Edge Processor data-quality + keyless Azure OpenAI auth" **Keyless Azure OpenAI (Microsoft Entra ID / managed identity).** Connect Azure OpenAI **without a static API key** — using a Microsoft Entra ID service principal or a managed identity, governed by your Entra tenant. Runs entirely server-side (no token reaches the browser), supports Public and US Gov clouds, and adds a one-click **Test connection** that names exactly what to fix if something is off. Connecting Azure with a plain **API key** still works on every tier; the keyless Entra path is an **Enterprise** capability. --- ### Edge Processor data-quality If your data passes through **Splunk Edge Processor** before it reaches Splunk, some parsing, timestamping, dropping and routing happens *upstream* — where Splunk's own internal logs and feed-health tools can't see it. This release teaches the assistant to look at that hop. - **New "Edge Processor → Splunk data-quality check".** Ask the assistant to check an Edge Processor feed and it reads Edge Processor's own operational metrics (throughput, dropped events, failed destination sends, and queue backpressure) and tells you, in plain language, whether data is being silently lost or delayed before it lands — with a proof dashboard. - **Honest by design.** If Edge Processor telemetry isn't reaching your Splunk yet, the assistant says so and gives you the exact setup steps (on-premises vs Splunk Cloud) instead of inventing a clean bill of health. It reports at the pipeline level and is clear that per-event checks need a small addition to your Edge Processor pipeline. - **Folds into the readiness verdict.** Edge Processor joins Splunk parsing, feed-health, and Cribl as another "is this data actually good?" signal, and can cap the Data Quality Score when it finds upstream loss. - Read-only and available on every tier, exactly like the existing Cribl check. --- ## 1.8.1 "Cleaner support diagnosis" A small maintenance update over 1.8.0 (front-end only). - **More accurate "Report an issue" diagnosis.** The automated issue classifier no longer mislabels a session that finished normally — one that completed and produced its dashboard — as having "run out of tool steps." The suspected-issue summary in your support bundle is now cleaner for healthy, tool-heavy sessions. --- ## 1.8.0 "Agent telemetry & OCSF export, content packs & all-tiers data quality" **New — your SOC can watch the agent (OCSF telemetry).** - **Adjutant AI emits its own activity as OCSF.** Every LLM call, tool / MCP / ServiceNow call, configuration change, unattended run verdict, and **policy refusal** (the proof the controls actually fire) can be written as open-standard **OCSF** events to a Splunk index your Enterprise Security / SOC already watches — mapped to CIM via the community **OCSF-CIM Add-On**. Your SOC monitors our agent the same way it monitors everything else: on-prem, with no cloud egress. - **You stay in control.** It is **off by default** and Enterprise-gated. **You provision and name the index** (the app ships no `indexes.conf`). Routing and content are resolved **per Organisation / Business Unit**; content export is denied by default and never exceeds your audit (DPIA) ceiling, with a server-side redaction check before anything is written. - **See it immediately.** A shipped admin dashboard — *Adjutant AI — Behaviour (OCSF)* — shows the token trend, model mix, tool/MCP egress with identity, the refusal and finding feeds, and a per-run drilldown, all on raw OCSF (no CIM Add-On required). **New — update Adjutant's content without waiting for a whole new app release.** - **Content packs.** Almost everything Adjutant does well lives in its **content** — the skills, knowledge, and playbooks. A **content pack** is a single, versioned file that lets us ship a corrected or improved content set straight to your install, and lets your admin apply it safely — no Splunkbase re-vetting cycle for a content fix. - **Your changes are protected.** Applying a pack **upgrades only the items you haven't changed**. Anything your team has customised is left exactly as-is and clearly listed, never silently overwritten — and your Org/BU scoping is always preserved. After an import you get a per-item report, and the list of items that need manual reconciliation is downloadable as a CSV. - **Safe by design.** Every pack carries an integrity check, so a tampered or truncated file is refused. Imports live on the **Backups** page, which also shows which content version you're currently on — run a backup first and you can roll back in one click. - **Retire without deleting.** A pack can mark an item **retired** — it stays installed but is hidden and switched off everywhere (it can't be picked, run, or used by the assistant). An admin can re-enable it at any time by removing the tag. **Improved — data-quality checks for everyone, and Splunk 10.x readiness.** - **Data-quality ingestion checks are now available on every edition, including the free tier.** Checking whether a feed is actually landing and parsing correctly — on `index=_internal`, through **TrackMe**, and through **Cribl Stream** — is a baseline capability now, not a Professional add-on. - **Ready for Splunk Enterprise 10.2 and 10.4.** The app declares Python 3.9 **and** 3.13 compatibility and has been audited against the 10.x platform changes (dashboards, the web framework, KV Store). Your admin still completes the standard KV Store engine migration as part of any 10.x upgrade. - **Smarter Dashboard Studio building.** The assistant now works from a single, version-aware map of what Dashboard Studio supports on **your** Splunk version — it won't reach for a chart type your version can't render, and when your Splunk is newer than what we've documented it builds conservatively and verifies the result. **Fixed.** - **Fewer false "the dashboard is blank" errors.** A heavy Dashboard Studio dashboard that renders fine but slowly is no longer wrongly reported as blank — the assistant confirms the panels actually returned data before deciding, so it stops wasting a retry on a dashboard that was already correct. A genuinely blank dashboard is still caught. - **TrackMe panels only when they belong.** Fixed a rule that pushed a TrackMe feed-health panel onto every generated dashboard (and used a lookup that fails outside the TrackMe app). The assistant now adds a feed-health panel only when it's actually relevant, using a method that works in your app. --- ## 1.7.0 "ServiceNow integration" (included in the 1.8.0 release) > **Renamed to Adjutant AI.** The app is now **Adjutant AI** (formerly "AI Workbench"). > This is a **display-name change only** — the in-app title (the easter egg now lives on > the dot of the "i" in **Adjutant Ai**), the app label, the documentation, and the > assistant's own self-description all say **Adjutant AI**. Nothing functional changed: > the Splunk app id, your saved searches/dashboards/models, KVStore data, and generated > artifact names are unchanged, so the upgrade is seamless. **New — run playbooks automatically, and from other Splunk apps.** - **On a schedule or on an event.** A playbook can run **unattended** on a schedule (a "morning health check") or in response to a Splunk event — an alert, an ES correlation search, or an ITSI episode. When an event triggers it, the affected thing (the host, user, or entity in the alert) is handed to the playbook automatically, so it investigates exactly what fired. Two ready-made (disabled) examples are included to copy. - **Adjutant AI as a building block for other apps.** Other Splunk AI agents can now ask Adjutant AI to **list** and **run** your playbooks through a small, safe interface (an MCP server). Only playbooks you mark **MCPready** are exposed, every call must name the Org/BU it is for (which must be a business unit you have set up) as a safeguard, and runs go through the same governed, bounded service — never an open door. This interface is **off by default** — turn it on with one setting. When on, the tools can also appear inside **Splunk's own MCP Server**, reachable on the normal Splunk web address (no special port needed); you authenticate with a standard Splunk token. A ready-made, read-only **example playbook** ships enabled so there is always something to see the moment you switch the interface on. **New — "Report an issue" support packaging (all editions).** - One click on any conversation (per-turn 🐞, the Ask panel, or the new **Help tab**) packages exactly what happened — versions, the resolved prompt, the tools and model used, the generated dashboards/searches, and every error and warning — into a single file. - **Safe by construction:** secrets are stripped before anything leaves the browser, and the file is **encrypted** to the support key, so it's safe to send over any channel. - It even **tells you what kind of problem it looks like** and matches known issues, so simple cases are solved without a back-and-forth. - **Send it your way:** download it and attach it to your own ticket, use the built-in support form, or email it. The **Help tab** (Report + Documentation + About) is always reachable — even if the app is locked by licensing. **New — ServiceNow, done properly** (Professional + the `servicenow` feature). Read incidents, changes, problems and the **CMDB/CSDM** in plain English — with bounded blast-radius / dependency traversals ("what's the blast radius if this CI fails?"). Turn a Splunk alert, ITSI episode or ES notable into a rich, deterministically rendered ServiceNow incident and **write the number back** to the originating object (a re-fire updates, never duplicates; the closed-incident policy is configurable). **Security incidents (SIR)** with MITRE ATT&CK, off until an admin enables them. Two transports (REST **or** a ServiceNow MCP server), plus TISC threat-intel enrichment — all server-side and allowlisted, so ServiceNow can never block the assistant. *(Verified against the documented APIs and unit-tested; final certification is on a live ServiceNow.)* **New — run playbooks automatically, and from other apps.** Playbooks can run **unattended** on a schedule, or from a Splunk alert / ES correlation search / ITSI episode (the triggering entity is handed to the run). Adjutant AI can also expose **list / run** over an inbound **MCP server** (off by default, MCPready-only, Org/BU-scoped) — reachable inside Splunk's own MCP Server on the normal web address, with a standard Splunk token. **New — "Report an issue" support packaging (all editions).** One click packages a failing conversation — secret-stripped and **encrypted client-side** — with an automatic problem classification, plus an always-reachable **Help tab** even when the app is licence-locked. **New — Cribl Stream data-quality awareness** (Professional+). Reads Cribl's own forwarded logs and metrics to surface the timestamp / parse / dropped-event problems that happen *inside Cribl, before Splunk can see them* — the "green in Splunk but timestamped wrong" blind spot — folded into one readiness verdict. No Cribl Lake or Search required. **New — LLM reliability: retry, fallback & circuit breaker** (Enterprise). A brief provider hiccup (503 / 529 / rate-limit) auto-retries within a time budget; a per-config **circuit breaker** stops hammering a provider that's down, then probes for recovery; and an ordered **fallback** transparently switches to your next provider (and tells you which it used). Two new admin dashboards — **LLM Health** and **AI Activity** — plus per-user / BU / org concurrency caps, all conservative and off the critical path. **New — live model & cost catalogue (all editions).** Models and prices come from a runtime catalogue that updates without an app rebuild; **automatic model discovery** (Professional+) keeps it current without ever logging your keys; an Enterprise admin screen adds price overrides and manual model registration for private gateways. **Fixed.** Generated Simple XML dashboards now share a single base search across panels (faster) and get a top data-ingestion health panel; corrected a 3× Opus price over-charge (now server-side authoritative, with Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 included). --- ## 1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth" **New:** connect to **OAuth 2.1‑protected MCP servers** (authorization‑code + PKCE for interactive, client‑credentials for unattended; tokens held server‑side, never in the browser — see [MCP_OAUTH.md](MCP_OAUTH.md)); **onboard new data sources** — describe a source or attach a sample file and get a deployment‑ready add‑on package; a **"is my data parsed correctly?"** ingestion/timestamp check that reads Splunk's own internal logs; generated config **validated against your instance** and given a **0–100 Data Quality Score** (A–F); and attach a local sample file in Ask (only the file name is audited, never contents). **Improved:** works with the newest OpenAI "reasoning" models incl. Azure GPT‑5.4 / GPT‑5.4‑mini (auto‑detects the request format); more reliable generated dashboards; generated objects use the **`aiworkbench`** name tag; and Audit‑tab improvements (Business Unit column/filter, local‑timezone timestamps, reliable token/outcome capture). --- ## Earlier releases (1.0.0 – 1.4.3) - **1.4.3** — Clearer guidance and plain-language fixes when a free-tier LLM key hits its provider limits (e.g. Groq token-per-minute caps, Gemini zero-quota keys); the LLM config screen flags these up front. - **1.4.1** — Per-feature capability licensing with edition badges (Professional / Enterprise / MSP); gated features show a padlock, and nothing you created is ever deleted when a tier changes. Everything it creates lands in the namespace of the app you opened it from. - **Some Data Foundation features need self-hosted Splunk.** The configuration-reference grounding and config-package generation (1.5.0) read files on the Splunk server, so they are unavailable on Splunk Cloud; the assistant says so and continues with what it can. --- *When a published fix resolves a tracked GitHub issue, it is summarised here with its issue number — for example: "Fixed: a dashboard panel could display raw HTML markup as text instead of formatting it (#123)."*

item.title: Riskability - v1.4.1 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
# Riskability 1.4.1 What changed since 1.2.3, the version on Splunkbase today. Grouped by what you will notice, not by commit. Nothing has been removed that you were using. ## In one paragraph 1.4.1 adds three optional layers on top of the scanner you have: an AI explanation of why each finding sits where it does, evidence from your own firewall logs about which ports traffic has actually reached, and rules a site can write to raise a finding the scoring signals cannot see. All three ship off. It also fixes three things that were silently wrong for everyone. Installers were being matched as installed software, and on a Windows laptop that was 40 percent of the open findings. A search head that received inventory before its first feed could report a completely clean fleet for up to two days, with no error anywhere. And an install that had never imported a feed could not reach the page that imports one. ## Fixed for everyone, on by default Installers are no longer software. A downloaded installer carries the installer's version, not the application's. Mozilla's stub reads as Firefox 18.05, the version of the self extracting archive it is wrapped in, and stood behind 2,101 open findings on one host. The collector has marked installers since 0.9.5; the app now applies the same rules itself to the fields every older collector has always sent, so no host is left out. Findings behind installers close with their own reason, installer_artifact or launcher_artifact, never as fixed or uninstalled, because nothing was fixed. On the test fleet 5,268 findings closed. Real software in the same download folder, a bundled Python and its packages, was untouched. Exposure is described as a stack of layers, not a socket. The exposure label is measured from how a process bound its socket, on the host, which cannot see NAT, firewalls or load balancers. The README and the pages now say so. A fresh install could report an empty fleet, in silence. The matcher runs at :17 past the hour and the host checkpoint at :30. Point a forwarder at the search head before importing a feed and the matcher runs with no feed, correctly finding nothing; the feed then lands; and the checkpoint credits every host with the feed generation current at :30 rather than the one the match actually used. Every host then looks up to date against a feed it never saw, the next match skips the whole fleet, and every page reads zero until a daily backstop comes round a day or two later. There was no error, no alert fired, and the pipeline watchdog reported success. This was found by installing the app on a Splunk that had never held it, feeding it through a real universal forwarder and leaving it alone for a full hour: the instance set up in the documented order produced 13,330 findings, the one that received data first produced none. The match receipt now records the feed generation in force when the match ran, the checkpoint stamps that rather than the clock's, and the watchdog fires when a host claims a feed that was imported after its own last match. Existing installations are unaffected on upgrade: a receipt written before this release keeps the previous behaviour rather than forcing a re-match of the fleet. A first run could not be configured from the browser. The app shipped unconfigured, so Splunk placed its own "not fully configured" page in front of every view, including Feed administration, and importing a feed was the only thing that could clear it. The app now ships configured and says for itself, on its landing page, when no feed has been imported. The upload control was never broken; it appeared the moment the gate lifted. ## New: AI prioritization, optional, off by default A model on your own hardware writes the reasoning beside each open CVE: why it is ranked where it is, what to do, concrete mitigations, and the ATT&CK techniques that apply. The score itself is arithmetic over measured facts, KEV, EPSS, CVSS, exposure and version evidence, and the model cannot move it. The page shows the scoring table, and a test fails if the page and the code ever disagree. What the page tells you. What is sent to the model, field by field, and what is not: no file contents, no account data, no other finding. What comes back and where each answer is used. Which rows never went to a model at all, because a rule settled them. Grounded, and checked. The prompt tells the model the measured facts are authoritative. Before that, on 5,755 real verdicts, the model called an internal finding internet facing in 19 percent of its explanations; after, on the same findings, 3 percent. Where an answer still contradicts the evidence it was given, the row says so beside the sentence, and the page reports the fleet wide rate. The priority is unaffected. Explain in depth. Any row can ask the model for a fuller explanation, written for a person. The answer is saved on the verdict and shared, so whoever asks first pays the model call and everyone after reads the stored answer, behind a green button, with Re-run beside it. Answers are rendered as headings, paragraphs and lists. The queue is usable at fleet size. Twenty five rows a page rather than every CVE at once, which on the test fleet was a page over a million pixels tall. Sortable columns, a word filter, and the reader's place kept when paging. Short columns are sized to their content. While it is off. The page tells an administrator the feature is switched off and where to switch it on, rather than showing a blank panel. ## New: network evidence and routes, optional, off by default If your firewall logs are in Splunk, the app can say per host and port whether a permitted flow from a declared entry point has actually been observed, graded confirmed observed, historically observed, unknown or not observed. It refuses to attribute a flow to a host it cannot tie to an address at that moment, and lists every refusal. Without a firewall source every row reads unknown, which is correct, and no priority changes. Routes. The jumps a permitted flow has been seen to make, drawn as a chain: entry point, host reached, port, software listening, findings open. Columns are hops, so a host reached through two others sits two columns in. Each jump carries the port and session count it used; a jump onto software with a known exploited or high EPSS finding open is red. Click any point to see the findings behind it on the same page. If no source is configured, the page says so and who configures one. Configured from the admin app. Index or accelerated data model, the field mapping, entry points with their scan pressure, and freshness. Test source says whether the data or the mapping is the problem. Show top 100 edges lists what the reduction sees before anything is saved. ## New: escalation rules A rule is a boolean expression over measured fields that raises a finding by one tier, for a risk the five scoring signals cannot see: a flaw in a library that a listening process actually loads, a product with no supported release and no fix. Five ship, all off; three name a field the app does not measure yet and are refused by name rather than run to no effect. Rules are switched on from the admin app, where a replay shows what each would move before it moves anything. Known limit: today only the AI expansion search applies a bump, so rules move nothing while AI is off. ## The configuration app Everything that changes how the app works now lives in the Administration menu, readable by admin and sc_admin only: Feed administration, AI analysis, Escalation rules and Firewall data source. Every write goes through Splunk's configuration service, so it behaves the same on a single search head and a search head cluster. ## Also fixed Saved AI explanations were being deleted hourly by a housekeeping job that rewrote a collection through a lookup missing those fields. It now deletes by key and touches nothing else. Changing the prompt or verdict schema did not invalidate the cache on a running instance. The analysis command now warns and names the page that fixes it. The firewall entry point macro failed with exactly one entry point declared, which is the common case. The Riskability Cycle dial on the landing page hid jobs. Every scheduled job was drawn at its own minute, so jobs sharing a minute stacked exactly on top of one another and only one could be reached. Ten minutes of the hourly schedule collide and :20 carries three, so eleven of forty five jobs were invisible. There is now one mark per minute, sized by how many share it, coloured by the worst outcome so a failure cannot hide behind a success, and its tooltip lists them all. Four panels showed token names rather than numbers on a first run. Splunk's stats command returns a row carrying only a count when it has one, and no row at all when it does not, so counters over an empty lookup left dashboard tokens unresolved and the page rendered the token's own name. Ten of them appeared across Start here, Fleet overview and MITRE ATT&CK on an install with no feed, no forwarder and no host. All nineteen views are now clean in that state. Explain in depth works for an analyst. The capability ships granted to the user and power roles, and the handler reads the endpoint settings, the stored secret and the verdict cache with Splunk's own system token, so granting it carries no other rights with it. A site that wants that decision kept with administrators removes the capability from those two roles. The AI settings page lists the models the endpoint reports instead of asking an administrator to type one, and Test analysis reports the fields the validated answer actually carries rather than failing on a renamed one. A screenshot gallery of every page is at https://chaugan.github.io/riskability/ ## Upgrading Replace the apps and reload. There is nothing to do on the forwarders. AI analysis, network evidence and every escalation rule are off after upgrading and stay off until an administrator switches them on, so an installation that ignores them behaves as 1.2.3 did, except that installer backed findings close on the next hourly run. No second archive is required. 1.3.0 had shipped the configuration pages as a separate app, which a Splunkbase listing cannot carry; 1.4.1 folds them back into the one archive as admin-only views, with the same restriction. TA-riskability-ai remains on GitHub for an indexing tier that installs archives rather than stanzas. The collector this release is built against is swinv 1.0.1; the oldest it tolerates is 0.7.1. If you are upgrading from 1.3.0, which was published on GitHub but never here, uninstall the separate riskability-config app after installing this one. Its pages are views of this app now.


Short Description:
Correlate the software your fleet already reports against offline CVE databases on a search head with no internet access. Ranks findings by exploitation likelihood and by whether the network can actually reach them. Track software that is already or soon becoming End Of Life!


Description:
Most vulnerability tooling cannot run where it is needed most. A search head with no route to the internet cannot call an API, pull a feed on a schedule or fetch a score on demand. Riskability is built for that machine. It takes the software inventory your hosts already report, correlates it against databases you carry across the air gap yourself, and answers what a CVE count never does: of everything found, what should somebody do tonight? CVSS says how bad a flaw would be if exploited, not how likely that is, and never whether your copy is reachable. WHAT THIS APP ADDS Exploitation likelihood. Findings are ranked by EPSS, the published probability of exploitation in the wild, and by the CISA KEV catalogue of vulnerabilities already exploited. Both arrive in the feed you import, never fetched live. Reachability, measured on the host. The collector reports listening ports and the process behind each, so findings answering a network address are separated from those answering only loopback or nothing. On a test fleet that turned 10,206 open findings into 11 that answer the network. It reorders the work. It never shortens it. Reachability, observed at the boundary. With your firewall logs in Splunk, the app can also say whether a permitted flow from the internet or an admin network has actually reached a port, and draw the jumps from entry point to the findings at the end. A site without firewall logs loses nothing. End of support. A CVE says a thing is broken; end of support says nobody will fix it again, which no advisory states. The app names software with no supported release. Rules your fleet needs. A risk the scoring signals cannot see can be written as a rule raising a finding one tier. Rules ship off, and a replay shows what each would move first. Optional AI explanation. A model on your own hardware writes the reasoning beside each finding: why it ranks where it does, what to do, which ATT&CK techniques apply. The score is arithmetic from measured facts and the model cannot change it. Where an answer contradicts the evidence, the row says so. WHAT IT REFUSES TO GUESS Every finding carries a confidence level describing the evidence, not the severity. A distribution that backports fixes without changing the version is reported as informational rather than asserted. A Coverage dashboard lists what the data cannot speak to, because a gap in visibility is not an absence of risk. Accepted risks go to an audit index written once, never rewritten. NO UNINTENTIONAL DATA OUT Nothing goes out unless you set up AI, and the recommended shape is a model in the same location as this Splunk instance, so nothing leaves the organisation. You build a feed bundle on a connected machine, carry it across and import it.

Install one free app and a real Formula 1 race is already moving inside Splunk. SPLap replays the 2025 Italian Grand Prix from real telemetry: 20 cars on a Monza map drawn from their own GPS, a timing tower with live gaps, every driver's speed, throttle, brake and gear, and race-engineer findings computed in SPL. Every panel has a Show SPL button, so the query behind what you are watching is one click away. A Grand Prix is a better SPL tutorial than another security log. Lap Delta Any two laps aligned by distance, corner by corner: braking point, minimum speed, throttle reapplication and the time gained or lost. Try Norris lap 48 against Piastri lap 47 and find the 0.207 s. Incident Review A 30-second evidence window around any race-control message, overtake or pit stop, with both cars on the map and their telemetry on one cursor. What happened next adds the stewards' trail for the same cars. Make your own call on lap 42, Turn 5. Race Engineer Ten deterministic rules (pit-loss anomalies, undercuts and overcuts, tyre degradation steps, closing rates, braking-point changes and more), each finding with a confidence, provenance, evidence and the SPL that reproduces it. No language model anywhere. Bring your own race Connect Data imports any historical session from the community OpenF1 API in your browser, loads an offline race bundle on an air-gapped host, or runs from a Python CLI. Imported sessions get every view Monza gets. Runs anywhere Nothing to configure for the bundled race: no setup page, no API key, no index, no token, no internet after install. Splunk Enterprise 10.x or Splunk Cloud Platform, AppInspect passed for both. About 4 MB. Free and non-commercial. Made on weekends by Lloyd Clark and his daughter Lilli, two F1 nerds who wanted a better way to learn Splunk. Repeats of the same malicious IP and direction are throttled for 45 minutes. * **Seven dashboards** for triage — Overview, Investigate, All detections, IP lookup, Trends, Alerts and Health — plus a guided Set up. ### Requirements * **A Criminal IP TI Feed License (API Key)** * Self-managed Splunk Enterprise on Linux. FortiGate is supported out of the box; Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS and Cisco ASA/FTD plug in through three search macros * A role with the admin\_all\_objects capability to save Set up * Outbound HTTPS from the Splunk host to dl.criminalip.io:443, and to hooks.slack.com:443 for optional alerting ### Known limitations * Splunk Cloud and Windows Splunk servers are not supported in this release: collection runs as a shell scripted input. * On a distributed deployment, create the cip\_ti\_matches index on the indexers yourself. The bundled indexes.conf creates it on a single instance only. * The raw firewall events workflow action matches on FortiGate raw field names. item.title: WithSecure Elements Add-on - v1.1.1 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
## Release notes — v1.1.1 **Enhancement release on the 1.1.x line** — targets Splunk Enterprise / Cloud 10.2+ (Python 3.13). Same fix backported to the 1.0.x maintenance line as v1.0.8. ### What changed The WithSecure Elements API now returns a top-level `mitre` array on each BCD detection that mixes ATT\&CK tactic IDs (TA\*) and technique IDs (T\*), e.g. `["TA0003", "T1518.001", "T1543.002", "T1059.004"]`. Previously only the `activityContext[].mitre_id` items were populated for cloud detections and the flattened `ac_mitre_id` field was aliased to `mitre_technique_id`. Two new search-time EVAL calculated fields on the `withsecure:epp:bcd_detection` sourcetype split the flat array by prefix: ``` EVAL-mitre_technique_id = coalesce(mvfilter(match('mitre{}', "^T[0-9]")), ac_mitre_id) EVAL-mitre_tactic_id = mvfilter(match('mitre{}', "^TA[0-9]")) ``` The regexes are disjoint: `TA0003` matches `^TA[0-9]` but not `^T[0-9]` because `[0-9]` requires a digit at position 1, and `A` is not a digit. `mitre_technique_id` falls back to the legacy `ac_mitre_id` when the top-level array is not present, so events indexed before the API migration keep working. `mitre_tactic_id` is a new field aligned with the Splunk CIM Endpoint datamodel, no legacy fallback needed. ### SOC-friendly queries this enables ``` index=main sourcetype="withsecure:epp:bcd_detection" mitre_tactic_id="TA0003" index=main sourcetype="withsecure:epp:bcd_detection" mitre_technique_id IN ("T1059.001","T1112") index=main sourcetype="withsecure:epp:bcd_detection" | stats count by mitre_tactic_id mitre_technique_id ``` ### Upgrade safety Non-destructive in-place upgrade. Search-time only — no ingestion impact, applies retroactively to detections already in the index, 100 % reversible.


Short Description:
Collects EPP Security Events and EDR Broad Context Detections from WithSecure Elements via OAuth2-authenticated API, with CIM-compliant field extractions for endpoint, malware, intrusion detection, and process data.

**New — Lost Request Tracing.** For the hardest kind of incident: a request that simply disappears, where the callee never responds and leaves no log. This screen instead records a **chain of custody across eight handover points** between the two hosts — from the app writing the request to the destination app handling it. The step where the chain breaks is the culprit; everything before it is cleared. A path map shows one row per affected segment, so you can see whether the request never left the caller, vanished between the hosts, or arrived and was dropped inside the destination. Steps it cannot judge are shown as unknown, never as passed — so neither the network nor the application is blamed by default.
